conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during your stay. You’re here because of left flank pain that’s been getting worse over the past week?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been hurting for a while, but lately it’s much worse. Feels like my old kidney infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned pain and feeling feverish, though your temperature was normal when you arrived. Any nausea, vomiting, or changes in your urine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. My urine’s been cloudy sometimes, but I always have that with my catheter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. Given your history of recurrent infections and the E. coli we found last time, we’re keeping an eye on that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t follow up after last time. I lost the appointment card.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’re going to check your urine again and run some blood tests to see if there’s an active infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But I’m not running a fever now, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, your temperature is normal. That’s one reason we’re being cautious about starting antibiotics unless we’re sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want the pain to stop. The Dilaudid didn’t help much in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll manage your pain. We’ve changed your Foley catheter today—that can sometimes help with discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, already? I didn’t feel it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was done while you were resting. We’re also watching your white blood cell count. It was a bit high earlier, but not extremely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your first urine culture came back. It shows mixed bacteria, which likely means contamination from skin or genital area.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s hard to say for sure. Because you have a chronic catheter, your urine often has bacteria. We’re more concerned about symptoms and other signs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But the pain is real.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’re not dismissing your pain. But we want to avoid antibiotics unless necessary, especially since you’ve had resistant bacteria before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the pain coming from my kidney?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure yet. We ordered a renal ultrasound to check for stones or swelling in the kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had so many CT scans. Are you going to do another one?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re avoiding another CT because you’ve had several in the past year. Ultrasound is safer and can rule out major issues like blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your ultrasound results are back. No stones, no swelling in the kidneys, and no signs of pyelonephritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be related to your chronic catheter or musculoskeletal issues. You have a history of back pain, and we found tenderness on your left side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But it feels like an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But your white count is coming down, you’re not febrile, and the ultrasound is reassuring. We don’t see clear evidence of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this time. Starting antibiotics without clear infection could lead to more resistant bacteria, which would be harder to treat later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your second urine culture also showed mixed flora—again, likely contamination. This supports that it’s colonization, not active infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Colonization?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—bacteria living in your urinary tract without causing infection. It’s common with long-term catheters.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep managing your pain. It’s already improving, and you’re not in distress. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if you stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I tested positive for cocaine again, didn’t I?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the urine tox came back positive. I’m not judging, but I do want to talk about how this affects your health, especially your kidneys and infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know, I know. It’s hard to stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can connect you with support services. Staying healthy includes managing substance use too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well—afebrile, pain is much better, and labs are stable. We’re going to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No antibiotics at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. We don’t see signs of active infection. Taking antibiotics without need can cause more harm than good in your case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adjusting them. Lower dose of amitriptyline and trazodone for sleep, and you’ll stay on fluoxetine for mood. Cyclobenzaprine for muscle spasms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the suprapubic catheter? You mentioned that last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We discussed it, but with your housing situation and follow-up challenges, it might pose more risks. For now, the Foley is safer because it’s easier to change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m trying to get into shelter. It’s just hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll help you connect with social work before you leave. They can assist with housing and follow-up care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I just want to stay out of the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We all do. Keep up with your care, avoid cocaine, and call if the pain returns or you develop fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for listening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. You’re being discharged home today in good condition. Rest, take your meds, and we’ll get the social team to check in with you.
